(Na​)=∏i​(pi​a​)ei​,

where each factor on the right is a Legendre symbol. The supplementary law is
(N2​)=(−1)(N2−1)/8.
(2)
For coprime positive odd m,n, quadratic reciprocity gives
(nm​)(mn​)=(−1)(m−1)(n−1)/4.
(3)
Applying this with m=3 gives
(N3​)=⎩⎨⎧​1,−1,0,​N≡1,11(mod12),N≡5,7(mod12),3∣N.​
(4)
Finally, factor d=2em with m odd. The supplementary laws for −1 and 2, followed by reciprocity on every odd prime factor of m, express (−d/a) solely in terms of the residue class of the positive odd integer a modulo d when d≡0 or 3(mod4). If a≡b(modd), all those factors, including the zero cases, agree; hence

In a linear model containing an intercept, the normal equations make the residual vector e orthogonal to every design column. In particular e⊥1, so
∑i=150​ei​=1Te=0
(17)
up to floating-point rounding.
The second design matrix has 49 random Gaussian columns plus the intercept, hence is a random 50×50 matrix. It has full rank with probability one because the determinant vanishes only on a measure-zero algebraic set. Its column space is then all of R50, so the fitted vector equals Y, the residual sum of squares is zero, and R2=1.

The transition rates of this birth-death process are qn,n+1​=λn and qn,n−1​=n(γ+βn). Thus, with p−1​=0,
p˙​n​=λ(n−1)pn−1​+(n+1)(γ+β(n+1))pn+1​−[λn+n(γ+βn)]pn​.
(18)
Multiplying by n, summing, and shifting indices gives
dtd​EN=(λ−γ)EN−βE(N2).
(19)
At a finite-moment steady state with positive mean and λ>γ,
βE(N2)=(λ−γ)EN.
(20)
Since E(N2)≥(EN)2, this implies
0<EN≤βλ−γ​.
(21)
If λ≤γ, both terms in the mean equation are nonpositive, and stationarity forces EN=0. Thus the population is extinct almost surely in any such steady state.

For any n with Rez>−n, define
F(z)=z(z+1)⋯(z+n−1)F(z+n)​.
(22)
The definitions agree on overlaps by the recurrence, giving a meromorphic continuation to C. Its only singularities are simple poles at 0,−1,−2,…. Since F(1)=1, repeated use of the recurrence gives
resz=−n​F(z)=n!(−1)n​.
(23)
These residues are nonzero, so all the listed singularities really are simple poles.

b

Words: 63 Articles: 1
7D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 63
b OurBigBook.com
The meromorphic continuations of F and the gamma function have the same recurrence and the same value at 1. Hence their residues at every nonpositive integer are the same. Their difference f=F−Γ therefore has removable singularities there and is analytic elsewhere, so it extends to an entire function. Equivalently, f(z+1)=zf(z) and f(1)=0 show inductively that the apparent quotient singularities are removable.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

c

Words: 102 Articles: 1
7D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 102
c OurBigBook.com
The product S(z)=f(z)f(1−z) is entire. From f(z+1)=zf(z) and f(1−z)=−zf(−z),
S(z+1)=f(z+1)f(−z)=−S(z).
(24)
Its modulus is therefore periodic with period one. The assumed bound for f on 0≤Rez≤1, together with the reflected bound for f(1−z), bounds S on that strip and hence on all of C. By Liouville's theorem S is constant, while S(z+1)=−S(z) forces that constant to be zero.
If f were nonzero at one point, it would be nonzero on a neighborhood, so f(1−z)=0 on an open set; the identity theorem would then give f≡0, a contradiction to that choice. Therefore f≡0 and F=Γ.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

Words: 82 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 82
b OurBigBook.com
For an expanding universe with 0≤w≤1, the coefficient (1+3w)H is positive. Thus Ω=1 is unstable toward the future: an initial 0<Ω<1 decreases away from one toward zero, whereas an initial Ω>1 increases and eventually corresponds to recollapse. In radiation domination, w=1/3 and
Ω′=2HΩ(Ω−1),
(34)
so a phase-line sketch has arrows away from the fixed point 1 on both sides. Consequently the observed near-flatness today requires extremely fine tuning of the early value of Ω.

(35)

The reduction map sends Hk​ onto Hk−1​ with kernel of order p, so ∣Hk​∣=pk−1. More explicitly, the lifting-the-exponent calculation
vp​((1+p)pj−1)=j+1
(40)
shows that 1+p has order pk−1 modulo pk. Hence Hk​=⟨1+p⟩ is cyclic of that order.
For the matrix claim, suppose A=I and choose m maximal such that A=I+pmB, so some entry of B is nonzero modulo p. Replacing A by a suitable power, we may assume its order is a prime q. If q=p, binomial expansion modulo pm+1 gives
Aq≡I+qpmB≡I(modpm+1).
(41)
If q=p, expansion modulo pm+2 gives
Ap≡I+pm+1B≡I(modpm+2),
(42)
because p is odd. Both contradict Aq=I, so A=I.
For p=2, r=1 fails because −I=I+2(−I) has order two. If r=2, the same argument works; in the order-two case, for maximal m≥2,
(I+2mB)2=I+2m+1(B+2m−1B2)eI,
(43)
since the parenthesis is nonzero modulo two. Thus the smallest value is r=2.

A language L satisfies the regular pumping lemma if there is an integer p≥1 such that every w∈L with ∣w∣≥p can be written w=xyz with
∣xy∣≤p,∣y∣≥1,xyiz∈L(i≥0).
(44)
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

b

Words: 76 Articles: 1
12J OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 76
b OurBigBook.com
Let a deterministic automaton for L have p states. During the first p input symbols of an accepted word w of length at least p, the run visits p+1 states, so two coincide. Write w=xyz so that y labels the nonempty loop between those visits and ∣xy∣≤p. Traversing that loop any number of times leaves the remainder of the accepting run unchanged, giving xyiz∈L for every i≥0.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
Zorn lemma says that a nonempty partially ordered set in which every chain has an upper bound has a maximal element. The axiom of choice says that every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. The well-ordering theorem says that every set admits a well-order.
Choice gives the Hausdorff maximal principle by repeatedly choosing an element extending a chain; the union at limit stages is again a chain. A maximal chain has an upper bound, and that upper bound is maximal, proving Zorn. Conversely, apply Zorn to partial choice functions ordered by extension. A maximal partial choice function must have the full family as domain, proving choice.
Choice also well-orders a set by recursively choosing from the unchosen remainder; Hartogs theorem forces this recursion to exhaust the set before it reaches the Hartogs ordinal. Conversely, from a well-order on the union of a family, choose the least element of each member. Thus all three principles are equivalent.

The Godel completeness theorem says that a first-order sentence follows semantically from a theory exactly when it is formally derivable from it. The compactness theorem says that a theory has a model exactly when every finite subset has a model.
Fix i. For each j=i, the theory Ti​∪Tj​ has no model because the model classes form a partition. By compactness, some finite Δij​⊆Ti​ is already inconsistent with Tj​. Let
Δi​=⋃j=i​Δij​,

a finite subset of Ti​. Every model of Ti​ models Δi​. Conversely, a model of Δi​ belongs to exactly one class Tj​; if j=i, it would model both Tj​ and Δij​, a contradiction. Hence it belongs to Ti​, and Δi​ finitely axiomatizes Ti​.

The space Cb​(R) is Banach because a uniform Cauchy sequence converges uniformly to a bounded continuous function. Compactness is essential: the algebra of bounded continuous functions having finite limits at both +∞ and −∞ contains constants and separates points, for example using tanhx, but its uniform closure has the same limiting property. It cannot uniformly approximate sinx, so it is not dense in Cb​(R).
